usage_notes.narrative: Carter prescribes maj7 chords as the I and IV members of the diatonic seventh-chord set ('Two major sevenths I and IV'), voiced in open rather than close position to accommodate finger span: 'the third of the chord has been moved an octave higher, and in the second case both the third and fifth have been moved an octave higher.' For voice-leading into the next chord, the bass note should be selected to continue a chromatic line rather than defaulting to the root. Chapter 9, pp. 117-120; Chapter 10, p. 120.

Carter prescribes open-position voicing as the practical solution for maj7 fingering: close-position seventh chords are defined but immediately redirected -- 'Unless you have long spidery fingers, you are probably more comfortable with these chords in either of the following standard alternate configurations' in which the third is raised an octave, or both third and fifth are raised. Chapter 9, p. 117.

Carter identifies minor sevenths as the II, III, and VI scale degrees in a major key ('Three minor sevenths II, III and VI'). In cycle-of-fifths practice, minor sevenths should be voiced with independent voice motion -- individual voices moving by half or whole step -- rather than root-position parallel block motion: 'If you think of harmonic movement as several moving voices rather than a glob of dots on a chord box grid, your arrangements and improvisations will be more airy, more interesting and less clunky.' Chapter 9, p. 117; Chapter 13, p. 156.

Carter prescribes the II-V7-I progression as 'the most common jazz progression unit' and the most idiomatic modulation bridge. The minor seventh on the II degree serves as the harmonic on-ramp before V7: 'putting a II of the upcoming new key in front of the new key V7' is the preferred jazz-language solution for connecting song sections and keys. Chapter 14, p. 166; Chapter 11, p. 141.

Carter identifies the half-diminished seventh (min7b5) as the VII chord of the major scale -- 'One half-diminished seventh VII' -- and classifies it among the four diatonic seventh-chord types. In ascending chromatic root-movement contexts, Carter prescribes the diminished seventh (dim7) rather than min7b5 as the connector. Chapter 9, p. 117; Chapter 10, p. 120.

Carter prescribes the dominant seventh (V7) as 'the most basic harmonic movement of jazz' and the mandatory gateway chord: 'The last chord of the intro must be a V7 or V7 substitute in order to move into the first chord of the tune itself.' For V7-I resolution, the prescribed voice-leading move is contrary motion: 'As the top note descends by half step the root note has its own opposing pattern, not parallel to the top.' Chapter 13, p. 156; Chapter 14, p. 160.

Carter prescribes V7 as the mandatory substitute for the final I chord when initiating a tag or coda: 'the replacement of the usual final I chord -- E, here -- with a V7 (or other substitute) chord is required.' The trigger is the cue 'Tag!' from the bandleader. Chapter 14, p. 164.

Carter prescribes V7 as the closing chord of every turnaround, treating the turnaround as 'practically another intro': 'Like introductions, turnarounds often start on a I chord and finish on a V7 or V7 substitute chord.' Chapter 14, p. 164.

Carter proscribes elaborate dominant-seventh turnaround elaboration when a singer is holding a note through the final two measures: 'About the only restriction is when you are backing a singer who is holding a note through the last two measures. You should then still be accompanying intelligently and not kicking out the jams.' Chapter 14, p. 164.

Carter prescribes rootless close voicing for dom7 chords in ensemble contexts: 'the accompaniment is voiced so that the harmony moves in alternating pairs of fourths and tritones. The bottom note in each pair alternates between major or minor seventh to major third. There is no explicitly stated root or fifth of the chord. If you play in a group, the bassist will cover roots and fifths.' Chapter 10, p. 129.

In cycle-of-fifths movement, Carter prescribes analyzing dom7-to-dom7 motion voice by voice rather than as root-position block changes. Using C7->F9 as the specimen: 'The middle voice moves by half step from E to Eb. The bottom line travels from C, the root, to A, the third of F9, by Bb, the 7 of the C7 note.' Chapter 13, p. 156.

Carter prescribes borrowing V7 from the destination key as the fastest modulation method -- achievable in as little as two beats: 'Presume you have ended a tune on the standard I chord and have used two beats doing it. You are moving to Db. Use the last two beats to borrow V7 (Ab7) from the upcoming new key, Db.' Chapter 14, p. 165.

Carter prescribes a specific bass-motion pattern for dom7 chords in spread texture: 'The root bass notes alternate in moving up a fourth and then down a fifth. Each new bass note is a tenth interval from the melody note above.' This produces the idiomatic 'spread' arrangement texture. Chapter 13, p. 157.

Carter prescribes a direct alteration rule for aug7 (dom7#5) and dom7b5 bass voicings: the major-scale shortcut for deriving the fifth 'does not automatically work with scales (or chords) that have raised (sharped) or lowered (flatted) fifths.' Instead, read the alteration from the chord name itself. Chapter 5, p. 77.
Carter's rule for aug7 (C7#5) bass voicing: 'If the chord is C7#5, raise the fifth a half step.' The plain major-scale fifth derivation is explicitly forbidden for this chord type. Chapter 5, p. 77.

Carter prescribes the diminished seventh chord as the standard connector for ascending chromatic root movement: 'In many cases the diminished seventh chord is the in-between, the hamburger helper of ascending harmonic movement.' Chapter 10, p. 120.

Carter prescribes chromatic approach chords -- including dim7 in the ascending direction -- as a recognized harmonic device: 'Approaching a chord from a half step above or below is another accepted way of moving the harmony.' Chapter 15, p. 167.

Carter prescribes a specific distributional rule for major triads in solo arrangement: 'when the melody is a major or minor third, the bass note is either a root or fifth, and when the melody is other than a third, the third is used in the bass to harmonically identify the chord.' Chapter 5, p. 83.

Carter's third-supply rule applies identically to minor triads: when the melody contains the minor third of the chord, 'no additional third is required -- the melody notes define the major or minor sound of the harmony.' When the melody does not contain the minor third, place the minor third in the bass to establish the chord's identity. Chapter 5, pp. 79-83.

Carter prescribes free stroke (not rest stroke) as the mandatory technique when harmonizing a major chord's melody with a note a third below, because thirds fall on adjacent strings: 'Since thirds are on adjacent strings, the free stroke must be used.' Chapter 6, p. 91.

Carter prescribes a strict voicing rule for sixth-below harmonization of major chords: 'By convention, scales harmonized in sixths have the key note of each scale on top, with the harmony note a sixth below. If the key note were in the bottom position the ear would perceive the scale as being in a minor key rather than a major key.' Chapter 8, p. 108.

Carter's key-note-on-top rule for sixth-below harmonization applies equally to minor chords. Diatonic sixths may imply minor sevenths or ninths; Carter permits adjusting 'the C to D if you wish to keep the sound to a simple Dm chord' when the extension is unwanted. Chapter 8, pp. 104-108.

Carter prescribes adjusting sixth-below harmonization when it implies an unwanted seventh or ninth extension on a minor chord: 'the sixth below will be the minor seventh interval C, of the Dm7 chord. The chord symbol above it is a simple triad, Dm. You can change the C to D if you wish to keep the sound to a simple Dm chord.' Chapter 8, p. 104.

Carter prescribes chromatic approach notes as the defining characteristic of jazz walking bass over dominant seventh chords. Bass-first conception is mandatory -- 'Think bass-plus-chord, not chord-plus-bass' -- because committing to a chord voicing first severely restricts available approach-note paths. Chapter 10, pp. 124, 141.

Carter prescribes whole-tone scale color as an option for dominant seventh chords specifically in intro construction: the example intro uses 'a little sprinkle of whole-tone scale thrown in at the C+7' before the final resolution. Chapter 14, p. 160.

Carter prescribes three standard ending formulas all resolving to the I (major) chord: 'V7-I, IV-I, and especially II-V7-I are standard.' The IV-I is identified as characteristic of soul and gospel music. Chapter 14, p. 163.

Carter prescribes the root/fifth alternation as the foundational oom-pah bass pattern under major chords: 'a root and a fifth are placed under each chord.' For variety, Carter prescribes mixed-rhythm bass (quarter, half, whole notes in combination) as the technique for 'de-emphasizing the oom-pah accompaniment while still using only root/fifth.' Chapter 5, pp. 76-78.

Carter's root/fifth bass pattern applies to minor chords with the same procedure as major: 'For Am, root/fifth is A, E.' If the chord has an altered fifth, the alteration must be read from the chord symbol and applied directly. Chapter 5, p. 76; Chapter 5, p. 77.

Carter prescribes moving tenths as the signature self-accompaniment device for major chords in stride-inspired solo playing: 'Moving tenths in the left hand was one of the primary accompanying devices of pianists in the swing era. Fats Waller, Willie "The Lion" Smith, Art Tatum, Teddy Wilson, and many others made this the style.' On guitar, Carter prescribes achieving 'at least half notes' for the moving tenths. Chapter 10, p. 127; Chapter 7, p. 98.

Carter prescribes independent rhythmic motion for tenths under dominant seventh chords: 'You probably would not use parallel tenths throughout the arrangement. For one thing, the melody would then have the same rhythm as the bass rhythm. The tenth does often function as a bass note, but only infrequently does it move parallel to the melodic rhythm.' Chapter 7, pp. 98-99.

Carter proscribes using parallel tenths throughout an arrangement: 'You probably would not use parallel tenths throughout the arrangement. For one thing, the melody would then have the same rhythm as the bass rhythm.' The prescription is to give the tenth its own independent rhythmic pattern. Chapter 7, p. 98.

Carter prescribes a bVI chord insertion after diatonic cycle movement as a deceptive cadence and modulation device: 'a bVI (Ab6) of the C scale is inserted. This deceptive cadence opens up several possibilities.' Chapter 15, p. 167.

Carter prescribes two-note inner-voice voicing as sufficient: 'A melody accompanied by two additional notes is often all you need to make an arrangement sound full, whether you are playing by yourself or with a group.' Chapter 10, pp. 125-126.

Carter prescribes back-cycling through the cycle of fifths as a systematic modulation method: 'Using the cycle of fifths as a method of movement, work backwards in the cycle to F7 and then C7.' Chapter 14, p. 166.

Carter prescribes tritone pairs as the primary harmonic accompaniment for sparse, ensemble-friendly solo arrangements: '3 on 4 takes its name from having many three-beat phrases in the context of 4/4 measures. The melodic line is primarily accompanied by tritones.' Chapter 15, p. 179.

Carter defines and prescribes the walkdown as a primary structural device: 'A walkdown is a descending bass line with a common tone on top of a chord stack. This is the device that keeps popping up in this tune along with its hook-like rhythm.' Chapter 15, p. 181.

Carter prescribes a strict ceiling rule for arpeggiated chord accompaniment: 'watch that your choice of arpeggiation doesn't reach higher than the melody, which might obscure the melody and confuse the listener.' Chapter 6, pp. 87-89.

Carter proscribes arpeggiation when the melody moves unpredictably by large leaps: 'If you notice that the melody of the tune you wish to arrange continually leaps up and down wildly, abandon arpeggiation for that particular tune.' Chapter 6, p. 90.

Carter prescribes that thirds harmonization alone is insufficient: 'A melody harmonized only in thirds can progress by itself for a section of a tune, but probably not for the entire song. Put the bass back in.' Chapter 6, p. 92.

Carter proscribes relying on thirds harmonization alone for an entire arrangement: 'A melody harmonized only in thirds can progress by itself for a section of a tune, but probably not for the entire song.' Chapter 6, p. 92.

Carter prescribes the ear as the final arbiter when a third-below harmonization lands on a non-chord tone: 'Non-chord tones make for the interesting spice in an otherwise dull chord-tone-only dish. It's your ear and your decision.' Chapter 6, p. 92.

Carter prescribes voicing all comping chords on the top four or five strings when playing alongside an electric bassist: 'If you play low-pitched, walking four-to-the-bar chords and your partner plays a walking bass line, it results in a muddy tangle of sounds. The solution is simple: play your rhythm part higher on the board on the top four or at most five strings.' Chapter 11, p. 135.

Carter prescribes a density rule for comping behind a soloist: 'play more when the soloist is not playing, and play less when he is. Play more when there are "holes" to be filled, and don't step all over the soloist when he is playing busily.' Chapter 11, p. 135.

Carter proscribes constant doubled bass notes for modern jazz style: 'Today the bass doesn't often play four quarter notes to the bar. Older-style bass playing included much doubling of two same notes per measure. Unless you want to recreate vintage jazz, avoid constant doubling.' Chapter 11, p. 141.
